title: AI's Potential for Access to Justice
author: Natalie Anne Knowlton · Sam Flynn · Tom Martin · Cat Moon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports AI’s potential to expand legal-service capacity and identifies bounded provider use cases, while acknowledging uneven task performance. But it does not substantively address the cluster’s principal claim that direct-to-consumer use shifts reliability and verification risks onto users with weak remedies, so its overall position on that proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source aligns with the proposition that AI could expand legal help through both provider-side capacity gains and bounded public self-help. It acknowledges uneven capabilities and unresolved privacy concerns, and presents these benefits as prospective use cases rather than evidence that AI can replace comprehensive representation.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core framing: generative AI may expand help for widespread unmet civil legal need through provider-side drafting, triage and intake, but its benefits remain prospective rather than demonstrated. Its call for experimentation, collaboration and care also aligns with the cluster’s cautious, augmentation-oriented deployment agenda.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source aligns directly with the cluster’s proposition: generative AI may expand legal understanding and legal-aid reach, but realizing that potential requires urgent preparation, careful experimentation and collaboration. It presents an implementation agenda rather than empirical evidence that AI has already improved access-to-justice outcomes.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The panel supports AI’s potential to expand legal information, self-help and provider capacity, while treating current applications as experiments and a copilot rather than demonstrated, autonomous solutions. Its proposed workflows and capacity claims align with the cluster’s view that useful uptake is plausible but do not establish sustained justice-gap closure.

So that when you're working on things, you take the output that it gives you as a suggestion, as something to get your mind going about solutions that you could come up with, to think of it as a co-pilot, to think of it as a collaborator.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Moon supports practitioner-led, cautious experimentation with generative AI rather than waiting for certainty. Her focus on extending legal understanding and legal aid’s reach aligns especially with the cluster’s access-to-justice agenda, while she presents these benefits as possibilities requiring practical exploration and care, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: So I spent a lot of time in my day job as Director of Innovation Design at Vanderbilt Law School thinking about how we can leverage technology to bring access to legal understanding information and really bridge this access to justice chasm actually that we face in the United States.

And so I thought we need to talk about this and how legal aid organizations and folks who are interested in bringing these tools to bear to serve more people, help them solve their legal problems, should be approaching these tools, things to think about, actual things we can do right now, concerns and maybe some heed and care we should take with these tools.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s view that AI adoption is an iterative service-design and learning process rather than a finished software solution. It advocates human-centred copilot use and practical experimentation despite professional apprehension, while offering little evidence on the cluster’s broader requirements around incentives, leadership, resources, connected data or demonstrated outcomes.

And people are going to have to take leaps of faith to get projects up and running and to start experimenting and to even potentially get funding.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with selective, human-centred deployment: it identifies bounded access-to-justice applications while stressing rigorous pre-release testing, interface guardrails and inevitable reliability limits. It also rejects treating AI as a remedy for deeper systemic defects, consistent with the cluster’s distinction between useful task-level assistance and broader outcomes.
qs: And I think the answer to that is just being really rigorous and testing the hell out of this technology before we launch it to consumers.
So I don't think necessarily that this is going to solve those systemic issues.

kp.k: Rapid capability gains prompted legal-tool development
kp.d: Tom Martin describes GPT as next-word prediction improved through human feedback and says ChatGPT surprised him despite earlier GPT-3 experimentation. Sam Flynn reports that Josef's machine-learning expert previously considered AI insufficiently ready, but GPT 3.5 and GPT 4 prompted development and launch of Josef Q. These are practitioner accounts of perceived readiness, not measured capability evaluations.
qs: So it literally calculates what's the next probable word based upon your request.
the responses that it's given out has been run through human beings who have given feedback as to whether or not it's a good response, and that feedback has been added to the training of the model
And as soon as we saw GPT 3.5 and GPT 4, we were ready to go. And so we actually built and launched a generative AI power tool called Josef Q.

kp.k: Legal aid workflows offer multiple proposed AI applications
kp.d: Natalie Anne Knowlton identifies prospective uses for legal aid and private practitioners: first drafts of public legal information, process guidance, intake and triage, translation drafts, audio and video content, community referrals, and consumer prompt-engineering education. These suggestions follow her inspection of an unnamed state legal aid website, rather than an implementation study. She speculates that enterprise offerings may address some privacy concerns and that controls will improve.
qs: So think about content generation, providing first drafts of content generation for external facing audiences with respect to legal information and how to navigate the flow of a process.
Triage and intake, I think there's a huge opportunity here to leverage these tools to streamline that process.
So can we use this tool, these tools to provide for first drafts of translation services?
I think some of the privacy concerns that we have seen so far may be addressed in the ChatGPT Enterprise Plan, but in any event, I think the privacy controls will only get better from here.

kp.k: AI could scale assistance beyond human-only provision
kp.d: Martin argues that human lawyers alone cannot meet unmet legal demand and that AI could expand provision through web, audio and video channels. His proposed mechanism combines scale with a bottom-up approach using the public's language. This is a claim about potential access to legal help, not evidence of demonstrated reductions in unmet need.
qs: So that ability to meet the demand, which is impossible through human lawyers alone, is something that AI can do well.
So it's not only web-based, but audio, video, every different method that we can get that information out there to help people.
including having a bottom-up approach versus a top-down approach, where we use the language that they use to provide information that's useful to them.

kp.k: Conversational retrieval could make static legal content usable
kp.d: Flynn describes an early-stage partnership among Josef, JustFix and Wilson Sonsini's technology subsidiary, named 650 in the transcript. Using Josef Q, the project aims to turn existing tenant-rights content into question-and-answer assistance searchable in everyday language. He identifies finding relevant information and understanding what to do with it as barriers to self-help; experimentation over the next few months was intended to establish results.
qs: it has a lot of static content that people struggle to understand, they struggle to find it in the first place, and they struggle to find the answer to their specific question, even when they're on the right page.
So allowing people to search for that information using their own everyday language, rather than the language of the lawyers who built out the content.
We're doing that project through our tool, Josef Q. And we're spending the next few months experimenting, seeing what the results of that application of the technology might be.

kp.k: Generative tools reportedly shorten consumer-tool development
kp.d: Martin contrasts supplying source information to generative AI with building hundreds of intents in systems such as Dialogflow, citing ongoing work including a State Bar of Arizona project. Flynn reports building a New York heat-law Q&A tool from JustFix FAQs in under five minutes and receiving correct answers to every question asked over the next 20 minutes. This vendor-reported demonstration supplies neither a question count nor an independent accuracy assessment, and supports a claim of faster prototyping rather than established deployment outcomes.
qs: For example, with an intent based system like Dialogflow, you might have to build out hundreds of different intents to answer different questions.
With something like this, you simply paste in the information you want it to be familiar with, and it could answer questions right out of the box.

We uploaded that into the large language model and trained it with a few questions and launched a digital Q&A tool in under five minutes that answered correctly and accurately every single question we threw at it for the next 20 minutes about heat laws in New York.

kp.k: Consumers may adopt directly before legal providers
kp.d: Knowlton is especially optimistic about consumer-facing use because she expects provider adoption to be slow and asserts consumers already use these tools regardless of lawyers' approval. She reports that a ChatGPT demonstration about divorce in Denver produced an accurate process workflow, contrasting this with static court and legal aid resources that describe topics without explaining steps. The accuracy claim concerns her demonstration, not a broader evaluation.
qs: when you're looking at lawyers and other legal services providers adopting and implementing, chances are that adoption is going to be pretty slow, if history has anything to say about that.
That's completely irrelevant to this conversation, because they are going to use these tools and they are using these tools.

So I did a demo the other day where I asked ChatGPT how I can get a divorce in Denver, and it came out with a list, one, two, three, four, five, six, however many there were, and it really was an accurate list of the workflow that one can expect when getting a divorce.

kp.k: AI assistance does not replace systemic justice reform
kp.d: Knowlton argues that the legal system has long been broken and does not expect AI necessarily to solve its systemic problems. She predicts it may make those problems' effects easier for consumers and does not expect it to worsen them. She recommends continuing systemic reform while redirecting professional risk aversion toward practical solutions for ethical, responsible use.
qs: So I don't think necessarily that this is going to solve those systemic issues. I also don't think it's going to make it worse.
So I still think that this shouldn't switch our conversation away from addressing some of those systemic issues with our system.
here are the issues that we see, here are the barriers, here are the risks, here are the concerns, but what can we do about them?

kp.k: Regulatory debates should center people needing help
kp.d: Martin characterizes ethics and unauthorized-practice concerns as excessively attorney-centered and calls for changes that make needed assistance legal and ethical. Host Cat Moon separately frames AI's speed as potentially forcing a reckoning with professional control of legal information, given limited access to lawyers. These are normative arguments and predictions, not descriptions of adopted regulatory reforms.
qs: I think there's a lot of attorney-centered concerns, right? Ethics, UPL, you name it. I think that's the wrong centering, right? It should be people-centered.
So we need to make changes, whatever they are, to make that possible, and to make it legal and ethical, to help make it ethical to be able to help people.
So I think the speed at which this technology is advancing to do good may force that reckoning to happen a little more quickly than perhaps we were anticipating.

kp.k: Consumer protection requires testing and explicit risk communication
kp.d: Flynn regards privacy, confidentiality and intellectual-property concerns as resolvable, often through contractual arrangements with technology providers. His principal recommendation is rigorous prelaunch testing of consumer tools, coupled with interface protections and context explaining reliability and accuracy risks. Moon endorses guardrails but questions how much control builders and lawyers actually have when consumers can independently access general-purpose tools.
qs: I think all of those are eminently resolvable, and lots of them relate to just the contractual arrangements you have with the tech providers.
I think the answer to that is just being really rigorous and testing the hell out of this technology before we launch it to consumers.

And if there are reliability and accuracy issues, which of course there will be, making sure we build into the user interface protections and context so that people understand exactly where the risks lie.
And I also wonder if this isn't giving us some false sense that we actually have control over any of these things, right?

kp.k: Existing search is proposed as a comparative baseline
kp.d: Flynn argues that consumers already seek legal answers through Google and speculates that Google gives wrong legal answers more frequently than ChatGPT. He supports this with a single informal defamation-law comparison in which he judged ChatGPT's answer perfect and Google's answers terrible, preceded by three advertisements. The transcript offers this as anecdote and conjecture, not comparative error-rate evidence.
qs: And how often does Google get the answer wrong to a legal question? My guess would be much more frequently than ChatGPT.
And I actually tested it on defamation law the other day, and ChatGPT gave me a perfect answer. And Google gave me terrible answers, which was preceded by three ads.

kp.k: Justice-gap estimates underpin calls for urgent experimentation
kp.d: Moon frames unmet need as affecting millions across economic circumstances, citing upwards of 80 to 90 percent of legal problems receiving no expert attention depending on study and jurisdiction. Flynn separately reports hearing that unrepresented parties in US civil cases rose from only 7%, or single digits, in the 1970s to 70% today and 90% for certain case types, using this to argue for urgency. Neither supplies study identification; these figures concern distinct measures and are reported claims rather than documented findings in the transcript.
qs: It can be upwards of 80 to 90 percent of legal problems are not attended to by any kind of legal expert.

I had the statistic the other day that in the 1970s, only 7% or in the single digits were unrepresented in civil legal cases in the United States. Whereas today, that number sits at 70% and for certain types of cases at 90% being unrepresented.

kp.k: Treat AI as collaborator, not perfect automation
kp.d: Martin recommends approaching AI as a creative collaborator or copilot whose outputs are suggestions, rather than expecting a flawless push-button solution. He argues that waiting until the technology is fully mature forfeits learning opportunities. Flynn advocates bravery in starting experiments and seeking funding, while Knowlton recommends preparing to use AI even under uncertainty about its eventual impact. These are adoption and learning recommendations, not claims that unsupervised legal advice is reliable.
qs: So the mindset that I suggest is the alternative to that, to view Chatch EPT and technology such as this as a creative collaboration tool.
you take the output that it gives you as a suggestion, as something to get your mind going about solutions that you could come up with, to think of it as a co-pilot, to think of it as a collaborator.
And people are going to have to take leaps of faith to get projects up and running and to start experimenting and to even potentially get funding.

So I would rather and I would rather for my colleagues in the legal profession to be on the side of being prepared and ready to thrive in this new environment, as opposed to not being prepared and finding themselves disrupted without any second thought.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers predict expanded legal-service capacity and more usable consumer information through generative AI, while distinguishing these opportunities from solving systemic justice problems.
pts.d: Natalie Anne Knowlton identifies potential applications in drafting public-facing legal information, triage and intake, first-draft translation, audio/video content, community referrals and consumer prompt guidance. She is especially optimistic about consumer-facing tools because they can explain procedural workflows and because consumers are already using them irrespective of lawyers' approval. Tom Martin claims AI can scale assistance beyond what human lawyers alone can provide, distribute information across channels and substantially accelerate the construction of consumer-facing question-answering tools. Sam Flynn describes using Josef Q to turn static legal content into answers searchable in everyday language, predicting a multiplier effect from faster tool development. Flynn also suggests ChatGPT may answer legal questions more accurately than Google, explicitly presenting the general comparison as a guess. Knowlton qualifies her optimism: AI may ease consumers' experience of systemic problems, but she does not expect it to solve those problems. Martin recommends treating AI as a creative collaborator or copilot rather than a perfect push-button solution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of practitioner experience, informal demonstrations and projects in development, rather than reported systematic evaluations of access-to-justice outcomes.
pts.d: Knowlton derives her internal-use suggestions from reviewing an unnamed legal aid website and supports her workflow claim with a personal ChatGPT demonstration about getting a divorce in Denver, which she judged accurate. Martin invokes seven years of LawDroid work with legal aid organizations and current implementation projects, including one with the State Bar of Arizona. His development-speed claim compares generative AI with intent-based systems such as Dialogflow, which can require hundreds of intents. Flynn describes an early partnership involving Josef, JustFix and Wilson Sonsini's technology subsidiary, identified as 650 in the transcript. He reports that a New York heat-law Q&A tool was built in under five minutes and answered every question posed during a subsequent 20-minute informal test correctly. No question count, independent assessment or downstream user outcomes are supplied. His ChatGPT–Google comparison rests on a personal defamation-law test. The speakers also invoke large unmet-need figures; Flynn recounts a historical increase in unrepresented civil litigants, but the transcript supplies no identifiable studies or methods for these statistics. These figures motivate the proposed applications rather than measure AI's effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opportunities are framed as immediately actionable in the source's 2023 setting, with near-term experimentation, slower professional adoption and explicit reliability safeguards.
pts.d: Knowlton contrasts consumers' present use with an expectation of slow adoption by lawyers and other providers, based on historical adoption patterns. She predicts improving privacy controls and tentatively suggests an enterprise plan may address some concerns. Flynn says the Josef Q access-to-justice project is in its early days and will be tested over the next few months; broader transformation is therefore prospective, not a reported completed outcome. He regards privacy, confidentiality and IP concerns as resolvable, often through provider contracts, but conditions responsible consumer deployment on rigorous testing and interface protections explaining reliability and accuracy risks. Martin conditions effective professional use on treating output as suggestions for collaboration rather than expecting instant perfection. Knowlton urges continued attention to systemic reform and preparation for potentially substantial disruption; no definite deadline or quantified forecast for that disruption is given.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal intended beneficiaries are people with unmet legal needs and the organizations helping them, with professional adaptation and consumer protection central to deployment.
pts.d: Knowlton's provider-side applications concern legal aid organizations and private attorneys, while her consumer-side examples concern people navigating legal procedures without lawyers, including divorce applicants. Martin emphasizes people currently unable to obtain legal help, who could receive information through web, audio and video channels and use it to make informed decisions. Flynn's JustFix example targets tenants seeking understandable answers about New York heat laws. These are access-to-justice and self-help claims, not merely enterprise cost-saving claims. LawDroid and Josef are presented as technology platforms enabling legal-service organizations rather than as alternative legal service providers delivering legal work. Consumer-facing Q&A is discussed separately from Martin's professional copilot framing; the transcript does not establish that every consumer answer would undergo human verification. Flynn highlights protecting end users against inaccurate or ill-considered tools. Knowlton also predicts that legal professionals who prepare for change will be better positioned than those who risk being disrupted through inaction.
